questions.article: Un-Islamic Culture in the Name of Islam
questions.q: The editorial recalls how Islam first spread in Bengal. How was it?
options: Through trade agreements with kings
Not quite. The article says: Through the peaceful work and influence of the Sufis.
Through the conquest of armies
Not quite. The article says: Through the peaceful work and influence of the Sufis.
Through migration from Arabia
Not quite. The article says: Through the peaceful work and influence of the Sufis.
Through the peaceful work and influence of the Sufis
Yes. That is why violence done there in religion’s name is called a tragic irony.
questions.rationale: “Historical accounts show that Islam spread in Bangladesh through the peaceful activities of the Sufis, who had a tremendous influence upon the populations of that region.”

questions.q: “Let us come to a word common to us” (Quran 3:64). What principle of social life does the article draw from this verse?
options: Begin any joint effort from what the parties already share, as the actual situation allows
Right. It is a matter of practical wisdom.
Insist first on one’s own position
Not quite. The article says: Begin any joint effort from what the parties already share, as the actual situation allows.
Wait until all differences have gone
Not quite. The article says: Begin any joint effort from what the parties already share, as the actual situation allows.
Avoid those who think differently
Not quite. The article says: Begin any joint effort from what the parties already share, as the actual situation allows.
questions.rationale: “The right way to begin any task involving social interaction is to find common ground between the concerned people, and then begin to operate within that frame of reference.”

questions.q: “Hajj is to stand in the plain of Arafat,” said the Prophet. What does the gathering there bring to mind, according to the article?
options: A great market or fair
Not quite. The article says: The Day of Judgement, when all will stand before God alike.
The Day of Judgement, when all will stand before God alike
Yes. All are in the same simple dress, saying the same words.
The armies of ancient kings
Not quite. The article says: The Day of Judgement, when all will stand before God alike.
The founding of Makkah
Not quite. The article says: The Day of Judgement, when all will stand before God alike.
questions.rationale: “The plain of Arafat, in which pilgrims spend one day, presents a picture of the arena of Judgement Day.”

questions.q: What does the article call the mark of a true pilgrim?
options: Returning with faith in God strengthened and rekindled
Correct. Otherwise it is only a tour.
Bringing home gifts from Makkah
Not quite. The article says: Returning with faith in God strengthened and rekindled.
Having travelled the longest distance
Not quite. The article says: Returning with faith in God strengthened and rekindled.
Having performed Hajj many times
Not quite. The article says: Returning with faith in God strengthened and rekindled.
questions.rationale: “To return from Hajj with one’s faith in God strengthened and rekindled—that is the hallmark of a true pilgrim.”

questions.q: The article says roses can be had only by tolerating thorns. What does this mean for unity among people?
options: Unity is not worth its cost
Not quite. The article says: Unity is possible only in spite of differences, not by removing them.
Differences must first be rooted out
Not quite. The article says: Unity is possible only in spite of differences, not by removing them.
Only like-minded people can unite
Not quite. The article says: Unity is possible only in spite of differences, not by removing them.
Unity is possible only in spite of differences, not by removing them
Well read. Their total removal is impossible.
questions.rationale: “In this world, unity is achievable only by learning to unite in spite of differences, rather than insisting on unity without differences.”

questions.q: According to the article, what shows an excellent character, as against a merely good one?
options: Behaving well towards those who differ from you or criticise you
Yes. Courtesy to the like-minded is easier.
Avoiding all discussion
Not quite. The article says: Behaving well towards those who differ from you or criticise you.
Agreeing with everyone
Not quite. The article says: Behaving well towards those who differ from you or criticise you.
Winning every argument
Not quite. The article says: Behaving well towards those who differ from you or criticise you.
questions.rationale: “If you behave properly with those holding divergent views from you or who criticise you, then you deserve to be credited with having an excellent character.”

questions.q: How should a believer conduct himself towards someone with whom he differs?
options: Break off relations until he changes
Not quite. The article says: Keep the difference to its own subject, continue the relationship, and stay free of ill-will.
Warn others against him
Not quite. The article says: Keep the difference to its own subject, continue the relationship, and stay free of ill-will.
Keep the difference to its own subject, continue the relationship, and stay free of ill-will
Right. Refusing to greet or meet the person is called improper.
Treat him as wrong in everything
Not quite. The article says: Keep the difference to its own subject, continue the relationship, and stay free of ill-will.
questions.rationale: “Mutual relationships should be maintained while continuing serious discussion on contentious issues.”

questions.q: Which of these did the Prophet say about a believer and his neighbour?
options: A believer should live far from his neighbours
Not quite. The article says: No one is a believer whose neighbour goes hungry while he has eaten his fill.
Neighbours are owed help only if they are relatives
Not quite. The article says: No one is a believer whose neighbour goes hungry while he has eaten his fill.
A neighbour’s affairs are no concern of ours
Not quite. The article says: No one is a believer whose neighbour goes hungry while he has eaten his fill.
No one is a believer whose neighbour goes hungry while he has eaten his fill
Yes. Nor one from whose hand and tongue a neighbour is not safe.
questions.rationale: “Nobody can be a believer, said the Prophet, if his neighbours pass the night hungry, while he has his stomach full.”

questions.q: If all people are equal, why are there differences of colour and race? What answer does the article give from the Quran?
options: They have no purpose at all
Not quite. The article says: They serve for people to know one another, not as marks of rank; the only merit is piety.
They serve for people to know one another, not as marks of rank; the only merit is piety
Exactly. God looks at the heart, not the body.
They show which peoples are older
Not quite. The article says: They serve for people to know one another, not as marks of rank; the only merit is piety.
They are the result of past deeds
Not quite. The article says: They serve for people to know one another, not as marks of rank; the only merit is piety.
questions.rationale: “Such outward differences are meant to serve as means of identification and were never intended as indicators of superiority… The sole basis of superiority in Islam is piety.”

questions.q: A dead body is washed, shrouded and laid to rest with great care. For whom, says the article, is this really meant?
options: For the family’s reputation
Not quite. The article says: For the living, who are reminded that the same end awaits them.
For the sake of ancient custom
Not quite. The article says: For the living, who are reminded that the same end awaits them.
For the dead, who feel the honour
Not quite. The article says: For the living, who are reminded that the same end awaits them.
For the living, who are reminded that the same end awaits them
Well read. They “experience death before death arrives.”
questions.rationale: “It has significance for those who are still alive. Through a dead person an important lesson is conveyed to living people—that they, too, will meet precisely the same fate one day.”
